report.polishedVersion: The hardest problem I solved was in the order page of our merchant console. Merchants said a competitor's console felt more responsive. report.contentContext: This is a strong, well-structured technical story. It follows a clear arc: initial assumption (perceived performance), first fix attempt with a concrete metric (code splitting, LCP 3.5s→2.6s), a surprising twist (the fix didn't resolve the complaint), a genuine investigative insight gained from observing real users, the correct root-cause diagnosis (redundant identical requests), the collaborative technical solution (stale-while-revalidate via Service Worker), and a quantified result (20ms cached reads, complaint resolved). It demonstrates technical depth, humility (initial assumption was wrong), collaboration, and a user-centered investigative mindset — exactly what strong interview answers need. Very little is missing; a one-sentence explicit callback stating the broader lesson learned (e.g., 'perceived performance isn't always about load time') would make the narrative arc even more memorable, but this is a minor enhancement rather than a gap.
report.languageContext: The response is fluent, idiomatic, and nearly native-level. Verb tenses are consistent and correctly track the narrative timeline (added, improved, realised, went through, used). Technical vocabulary (code splitting, LCP, stale-while-revalidate, Service Worker, request logs) is used precisely and naturally. Sentence structure varies well and connectors (when, that's when, with) create logical flow without feeling choppy or overly formal. There are no grammar mistakes, awkward collocations, or article/preposition errors. report.polishedVersion: The hardest problem I solved was on the order page in our merchant console. Merchants said a competitor's console felt more responsive. I added code splitting, and LCP improved from about 3.5 seconds to 2.6 seconds, but the complaint was still there. When our team visited some merchants, I saw them run the same filter hundreds of times a day, reload the page, and keep several tabs open. That's when I realised I was measuring the wrong thing — the real problem was the same request being made again and again. Together with a senior engineer, I went through the request logs, and we implemented stale-while-revalidate caching in a Service Worker. A cached read came back in about 20 milliseconds, and the complaint went away.

report.polishedVersion: At ByteDance, we built a word cloud of the top keywords in video comments. When you hovered over a keyword, a tooltip showed its stats. Inside that tooltip, there was a second tooltip. I talked to the PM about it, because the analysts needed to compare keywords. If your mouse slipped, both tooltips would close, and you couldn't keep two open side by side. I didn't just say no. I suggested a modal, so they could read and compare the details. The PM wanted the detail close to the chart, so we met in the middle: we added a 'View details' link to the tooltip, and it opened the details in a panel next to the chart. I learned to disagree about the user, not about my own taste.

report.polishedVersion: When I worked at ByteDance, I took on a requirement to implement a cloud chart with a tooltip. There was a second tooltip inside the first one that appeared when I hovered over the data, and it just showed comparison data. However, it was a little unsuitable for the client. We had a discussion, and then I shared a new design with the PM. It used a modal to show the comparison data, but she thought it was too complicated. Reflection: I think we should focus more on how users can use the product comfortably, instead of just pushing our own best design.
